children.html: The factor structure and psychometric properties of an Arabic-translated version of the Body Appreciation Scale-2
Zahir Vally PhD Caroline G. D'Souza BA Hiba Habeeb BA
Department of Psychology and Counseling, United Arab Emirates University, Al Ain, United Arab Emirates
Zahir Vally, PhD, Department of Psychology and Counseling, United Arab Emirates University, P.O. Box 15551, Al Ain, United Arab Emirates. Email: zahir.vally@uaeu.ac.ae

Purpose: The conduct of body image studies with Arab populations is hindered by a lack of psychometrically sound assessment measures. We examined the psychometric properties of an Arabic translation of the most frequently employed measure of body appreciation, the Body Appreciation Scale-2 (BAS-2).

Design and Methods: A sample of college-aged women from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) (n = 256) completed the Arabic BAS-2, and measures of aesthetic and functional body image, authentic body pride, and self-reported body mass index (BMI).
Results: Exploratory factor analysis revealed that the Arabic BAS-2 had a one-dimensional factor structure. BAS-2 scores were positively correlated with body image and body pride, but not with BMI.

Practice Implications: A psychometrically sound BAS-2 may now facilitate the conduct of crosscultural work that includes the Arabic-speaking population, an often-neglected ethnic group in most body image studies.
Arabic translation, body appreciation scale, factor structure, reliability, validity

Scholars engaged in the study of body image and disordered eating have increasingly turned to concern themselves with the study of body appreciation,1 a primary component of positive body image, that is defined as love for and comfort with one's body, endorsement of a broad idea of attractiveness, engaging in adaptive self-care, and the manifestation of positive feelings in one's body.2 Body appreciation is most frequently measured using the Body Appreciation Scale-2 (BAS-2).3 This most recent iteration of the scale was developed to address issues related to its reported lack of cross-cultural validity.4 The current 10-item BAS-2 has demonstrated satisfactory psychometric properties, including a consistent single factor structure, adequate internal consistency, good test–retest reliability, and adequate construct validity across a number of varying linguistic and cultural contexts including in China,5 France,6 Iceland,7 Iran,8 Holland,9 Serbia,10 Spain,11 Poland,4 and the United States.3

As a contribution to the literature, we undertook to develop and investigate the psychometric properties of an Arabic-translated version of the BAS-2 as this had not previously been done. This is a worthwhile endeavor given that the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the location of the present study, has experienced exponential social and economic growth in recent years. This is noteworthy as previous research indicates that increased modernization of a society and greater exposure to consumerist-oriented Western media is invariably followed by the promotion of an idealized and stereotyped notion of beauty, and, this phenomenon is further amplified where greater integration between the existing host culture and a large Western expatriate population occurs.12 Also, no studies have, thus far, investigated body appreciation as a construct in an Arab population. Thus, establishing the psychometric properties of the BAS-2 in this population will facilitate the conduct of cross-cultural studies in which Arab samples are included, and, more generally, the promotion of body image studies in this region of the world.

The present study sought to investigate the following hypotheses. First, most previous investigations of the factor structure of the BAS-2 have found a one-factor structure.1,11 We expected, following an exploratory factor analysis (EFA), that our Arabic version would also yield a similar result. Second, participants completed additional measures of body image and body pride which enabled an analysis of the convergent validity of the BAS-2. We hypothesized, in line with previous investigations,3–5,8 that scores on the Arabic BAS-2 would be significantly and positively associated with scores on the body image and body pride measures but negatively associated with body mass index (BMI) which we ascertained through self-report of height and weight. We also report on the internal consistency of all the measures.

This study employed a cross-sectional survey design and a convenience sample of 256 undergraduate female students enrolled at a large, public university in the UAE. Participants were recruited from undergraduate psychology and general education courses and received course credit for participation. Participants ranged in age from 18 to 26 (M = 20.35 years, SD = 1.81) and in self-reported BMI from 14.27 to 49.42 kg/m2 (M = 22.98, SD = 5.01). The sample was ethnically homogenous, all participants were of Arab descent, and identified as Muslim.

Participants self-reported their height in meters and their weight in kilograms and these were used to compute BMI as kg/m2. There is evidence to suggest that self-reported height and weight are as reliable as data measured using objective means.13

Participants were asked to complete an Arabic-translated version of the BAS-2,3 a 10-item scale that assesses acceptance of, respect, and care for one's body, as well as protection from unrealistic standards of beauty. Items are rated on a 5-point scale, ranging from 1 (Never) to 5 (Always), and an overall score computed as the mean of the 10 items with higher scores on this scale being reflective of greater body appreciation.3 The BAS-2 has shown satisfactory reliability and validity in samples from a range of diverse socio-cultural contexts.6,8,11

The 6-item Authentic Pride subscale of the Body and Appearance Self-Conscious Emotions Scale (BASES14) measures body pride as a sense of personal appearance-related achievement (sample item: "I am proud of my appearance efforts"). Responses to the six items are rated on a 5-point scale, ranging from 1 (Never) to 5 (Always), and averaged such that higher scores are reflective of greater authentic body pride. There
is supportive evidence of the measure's factor structure, validity, test– retest reliability, and internal consistency in Western samples.14

Body image was measured using the Embodied Image Scale (EIS)15 which measures the cognitive, behavioral, and affective components of body image, and incorporates both the functional and aesthetic dimensions of the body. Functional body image refers to the extent to which individuals place value on, invest in, and evaluate their bodies as a functional tool for what it is capable of doing. On the other hand, aesthetic body image refers to the extent to which the body is valued, invested in, and evaluated based on its external appearance. The EIS consists of 17 items measuring six subscales. Example items include "How good I feel about my body depends a lot on whether people consider me good-looking" and "How good I feel about my body depends a lot on what my body can do physically." In Western samples of both men and women, the EIS and its subscales have demonstrated adequate internal consistency ( = .72–.90), acceptable predictive validity in relation to self-esteem and depressed mood, and satisfactory discriminant validity.15,16

Students were recruited from a range of undergraduate psychology and general education classes. The project was advertised as "a study about body image." The three questionnaires were administered using the Qualtrics online survey platform. The survey first provided background information about the study, participant rights within the context of the study (e.g., voluntary participation, right to withdraw at any time without prejudice), issues pertaining to confidentiality of the information provided, and included the primary investigator's contact details in the event that any questions arose prior to or after completion of the survey. Participants then completed an informed consent form, which was displayed on the screen, clicking to proceed ahead was taken as the provision of consent to participate. Participants were then directed to the three assessments described above, which were always presented in the same sequence.

All scales were carefully translated from English to Arabic using the following 5-step process outlined by Brislin17: (1) Two teams of students each consisting of a psychology and a translation major student who were fluent in both English and Arabic translated the items from English to Arabic resulting in two versions of the translated BAS-2. (2) Then, a third team with the same composition of knowledge and linguistic expertise evaluated the two versions from step 1 comparing their semantic and linguistic characteristics, and identified any discrepancies which were discussed between the three teams and final item translations chosen using consensus. A single Arabic version of the scale was thus constituted as a result of this comparative process. (4) A bilingual psychology professor with substantial expertise in the translation of psychological assessment measures translated this Arabic version back into English. (5) The first author examined the Arabic-translated document and the back-translated version and concluded that there were no substantial differences between the Arabic version of the measure and its original English version. 3.1 Principal-axis factor analysis of the BAS-2

A highly significant Bartlett's test of sphericity (2 = 1437.80, df = 45, p < .001) and a Kaiser—Meyer–Olkin (KMO) value of .93 indicated that the BAS-2 data had adequate factorability. The results of the factor analysis indicated that only a single factor should be extracted. This factor had an eigenvalue of 5.69 and explained 56.89% of the total variance. All 10 items of the BAS-2 loaded onto this single factor and exhibited factor loadings that were fair to excellent20 (Table 1 displays the item-factor loadings and corresponding Arabic translation for each of the items).
3.2 Principal-axis factor analysis of body pride and body image measures

No Arabic version of the BASES was available at the time of the study. Therefore, we prepared our own translation and examined its factor structure using a principal-axis EFA with quartimax rotation of the total sample. The data indicated that this subscale had adequate factorability (Bartlett's test of sphericity, 2 = 532.657, df = 10, p < .001, and KMO = .86). Results indicated the presence of a single factor with

an eigenvalue of 3.85 and explaining 77% of the total variance. All factor loadings were excellent (.73–.91). Similarly, no Arabic version of the EIS exists. We translated the original version and assessed its factor structure using principal components extraction with varimax rotation. A significant Bartlett's test of sphericity (2 = 1134.74, df = 136, p < .001) and a KMO value of .84 suggested that these data had adequate factorability. The data indicated that three factors should be extracted accounting for 64% of the variance. Thus, we included all items in the ensuing analyses.

Cronbach's alpha () coefficients ranged from .89 to .92, all representing reliability coefficients in the good to excellent range using George andMallery's18 rules of thumb. Table 2 provides an analysis of the itemtotal statistics and Cronbach's values if each individual item were to be deleted. Reliability would remain good to excellent. To assess the convergent validity of the BAS-2, we used Pearson correlation coefficients to assess the association between body appreciation, BMI, body pride, and body image. BAS-2 scores were significantly and positively correlated with body pride (r = .467, p < .001), and body image (r = .459, p < .001), and negatively correlated but not significantly so with BMI (r = –.04, p > .05), in sum providing preliminary evidence of good convergent validity for the BAS-2 (see Table 3 for the full correlation matrix and all internal consistency coefficients).

This study aimed to assess the factor structure and psychometric properties of an Arabic-translated version of the BAS-2. An EFA supported the presence of a one-dimensional factor structure for the BAS-2. This is in accordance with the original English version3 as well as other translated versions in a variety of different languages.4–10 Our convenience sample of females limited any exploration of sex differences in the presentation of body appreciation in this locale. This, therefore, remains a worthwhile focus for future studies, especially when considering that the totality of evidence examining the differential gendered reporting of body appreciation remains equivocal. Most studies report higher scores in men compared to women;8,19 however, some have reported no significant differences between men and women.6,19 These inconsistent results necessitate the further examination of sex differences in body appreciation, particularly for individuals from varying ethnic and cultural groups as less is known about samples outside first-world, Western contexts.

Furthermore, our analyses also provide evidence of the BAS-2′ s internal consistency and convergent validity. Correlation coefficients between scores on the BAS-2 and the BASES and EIS, respectively concur with those of previous studies.4,8,9 Body appreciation scores were positively correlated with scores on authentic body pride and body image. The correlation between body appreciation and BMI was not significant but the coefficient was negative. As in other parts of the

world, our results suggest that for the present sample, individuals who appreciate, love, and possess respect for their bodies are more likely to present with a healthier overall body image as well as pride for their bodies, both for its aesthetic and functional capacities.

Despite these promising findings, the following limitations should be noted. First, our use of a convenience sampling method results in a very specific sample, young adult women attending a university. Moreover, Arab people are not a homogenous group and thus our findings may not pertain to individuals beyond this particular profile. Second, there remains the possibility that the sample's BMI data may not be accurately captured as we relied on participant self-report of their height and weight. However, most studies in this domain of research rely solely on self-report data to compute BMI as it has been shown to be as reliable as objective height and weight measurements.13 Third, while test–retest reliability may have been a more preferable measure of reliability than internal consistency, the design of our study did not allow for a second administration point. Reporting on the instrument's internal consistency using Cronbach's values is also in keeping with the norm of similar BAS-2 psychometric studies in other languages.6,8,11 In conclusion, despite these potential study limitations, the Arabic version of the BAS-2 appears to be a reliable and valid measure of body appreciation when used with an Arabic-speaking population in the UAE.
